paras: The hanging of a soldier at Gardiner, Montana, took place on August 29, 1888, when townspeople put a rope around the neck of an unnamed army recruit accused of robbing the house of a dead woman and hung him up until he confessed. He survived, the stolen goods were recovered, and he was handed over to his commander for military discipline. Papers across the West and Midwest carried the story as the climax of reports about a troublesome batch of recruits, and a Montana paper said residents regretted he had not been hanged to death.

Sixteen recruits had recently been sent from Fort Keogh to the garrison under Captain Harris at Mammoth Hot Springs. According to the Livingston dispatches, several had deserted, six were in the guard house, and one had been sent away to be court-martialed. The day before the Gardiner incident, another recruit defied an officer and was forced back to camp at gunpoint; the Livingston Enterprise placed this at the Mammoth Hot Springs hotel and named the officer as Lieut. Tutherly.

On Wednesday one of the recruits went to Gardiner and asked to see the remains of Mrs. Metcalf, who had died the day before, claiming to have known her years earlier. After he left, a gold watch, a valise and money were missing; the River Press called the bag a satchel, and the Enterprise added some gold dust. People from the house of mourning searched for him, and he was caught, but he had already hidden the goods and denied knowing where they were.

The wire dispatch said only that a rope was placed around his neck and he was 'nearly lynched' before he confessed. The Montana accounts were more specific: according to the Livingston Enterprise, 'a few determined men' put a rope around his neck and swung him to a neighboring beam, and after several jerks he confessed. The River Press said it took 'several severe jerks' to make him tell all.

The property was recovered, and the private was turned over to Captain Harris and the garrison authorities for military discipline, in the River Press's words 'more dead than alive'. No report of an arrest or prosecution of the men who hanged him appears in the coverage, and none of the papers names the soldier or reports the outcome of his discipline.

The story reached readers through a Livingston dispatch that appeared on August 30 in the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Rock Island Argus and the Beatrice Daily Express, and later in the Yankton Press and Dakotaian and the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner. Its headlines were about the soldiers rather than the hanging: 'SOME BAD SOLDIERS', 'A BAD LOT OF RECRUITS', which 'Make Life a Burden for Citizens of a Montana Town', and 'REBELLIOUS REGULARS'.

Montana papers wrote with open approval of the townspeople. The Livingston Enterprise described the soldier as 'devoid of the slightest feelings of manhood' and said he was handed to 'the tender mercies of Captain Harris for further treatment'. The River Press, under the headline 'A TOUGH LOT', ended its account by noting that regrets were 'freely expressed that he was not hanged to the finish of his miserable life'. That version was reprinted in the Emporia Weekly News, which dropped the closing line, and in the Dakota Reporter and Farmer, which rendered it as regret that he was 'not hung outright'.
None of the papers mentioned the soldier's race or that of the men who hanged him.

reader.title: Hanging of a soldier at Gardiner, Montana
bases: Men at Gardiner put a noose around a soldier's neck and hung him up until he confessed to a theft, an attempted or near lynching in which no one died (A1, A6, A7).

The soldier survived and was turned over to his commander (A1, A6, A7); the men acted without legal authority to punish and force a confession over a theft, but no one was killed, and the group is described only as 'citizens' or 'a few determined men' (A1, A6).

The wire dispatch (A1, A2, A3) and the local Livingston Enterprise account (A5, A6) agree that a recruit was accused of stealing from a dead woman's house at Gardiner and was hanged by a rope until he confessed; the River Press (A7) gives a third, more detailed version.

accounts.label: Wire dispatch (Livingstone)
accounts.gist: Citizens captured the recruit after he hid the goods; a rope was placed around his neck and he was 'nearly lynched' before he confessed, then turned over to the garrison.

accounts.label: Livingston Enterprise (local)
accounts.gist: He was suspected, followed and denied the theft; a few men put a rope around his neck and swung him to a beam, and after several jerks he confessed and was turned over to Captain Harris.

accounts.label: River Press (Livingston, Aug. 29)
accounts.gist: A few determined men hung him up by a noose with 'several severe jerks' until he confessed; he was handed to Captain Harris 'more dead than alive', and people regretted he was not hanged to death.

framing.detail: Out-of-state papers ran the wire under headlines about the soldiers, 'SOME BAD SOLDIERS', 'A BAD LOT OF RECRUITS', 'REBELLIOUS REGULARS', with the near lynching as one item.
The Livingston Enterprise called the soldier 'devoid of the slightest feelings of manhood' and said he went to 'the tender mercies of Captain Harris for further treatment'.
The River Press, under 'A TOUGH LOT', closed by saying regrets were freely expressed that he was not hanged 'to the finish of his miserable life'.

info: Wednesday, August 29, 1888: Livingston dispatches dated Aug. 29 say 'today' and the Enterprise says 'Wednesday'.
Gardiner, Montana, at the house where Mrs. Metcalf's body lay; the Enterprise says he was swung 'to a neighboring beam'.
An unnamed private, one of sixteen recruits sent from Fort Keogh to the garrison under Captain Harris at Mammoth Hot Springs; race not stated.
Accused of stealing a gold watch, a valise (or satchel) and money, and in the Enterprise also gold dust, from the room where the dead Mrs. Metcalf lay, after asking to view her remains.
'Citizens' (wire) or 'a few determined men' (River Press, Enterprise) of Gardiner; none named.
The stolen property was recovered and the soldier was turned over to Captain Harris and the garrison for military discipline.
